articles.title: Nvidia stock plunges after hours as New York Times reports new Jensen Huang relationship allegation
articles.desc: WOW "NVIDIA PREPARING TO OUST NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG": WSJ NVDA shares reverse Wednesday's gains following a report that Nvidia's CEO had a relationship with an executive reporting to him. If confirmed, the allegations could add a new corporate-governance problem to the company's existing leadershi
articles.content: WOW "NVIDIA PREPARING TO OUST NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG": WSJ NVDA shares reverse Wednesday's gains following a report that Nvidia's CEO had a relationship with an executive reporting to him. If confirmed, the allegations could add a new corporate-governance problem to the company's existing leadership controversy. Nvidia (NVDA) shares are falling sharply in after-hours trading following a new report from The New York Times alleging that CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a company executive who reports to him. According to a market quote captured at 00:11 GMT+2 on November 12, NVDA traded at $167.37 after hours, down $6.36 or 3.66% from Wednesday's regular-session close of $173.73. The decline reverses more than Wednesday's 2.87% regular-session gain. Why the latest Nvidia allegations matter to investors The New York Times reported the new allegation late Wednesday, adding another potential complication for Nvidia's board of directors. The company is already investigating Huang following earlier reports concerning his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly identified as having connections to Chinese intelligence. That earlier controversy raised questions about national security, corporate oversight and whether sensitive information could have been compromised. The latest allegation, however, introduces a potentially different concern. If Huang had a relationship with an executive who reported directly to him, investors could reasonably question whether there were conflicts of interest involving management decisions, compensation, promotions or internal corporate governance. A personal relationship does not, by itself, establish wrongdoing or improper conduct. The significance depends on the circumstances, the company's policies, what was disclosed to the board and whether any business decisions were affected. The new allegation has not been independently verified by investingLive. Why Nvidia stock could face additional pressure Jensen Huang is not an ordinary corporate CEO. He co-founded Nvidia and has been central to its transformation into one of the world's most important artificial intelligence companies. For shareholders, the concern is not simply the executive's personal conduct. It is whether repeated controversies could undermine confidence in Nvidia's leadership, distract management or increase pressure on its board. There are three particularly important implications. Corporate governance: Investors may demand clearer answers about how Nvidia's board oversees its CEO and manages potential conflicts of interest. Leadership continuity: Any widening of the investigation could raise further questions about succession planning at a company closely associated with its founder. Valuation and investor confidence: Even without changes to Nvidia's chip demand, earnings or competitive position, greater uncertainty about leadership could influence how much investors are willing to pay for the stock. That does not mean Huang will leave Nvidia or that the allegations will ultimately affect the company's operations. But investors may increasingly distinguish between confidence in Nvidia's AI business and confidence in its corporate leadership. What NVDA traders should watch next The immediate question is whether the after-hours selling continues when regular U.S. trading resumes Thursday, November 12. The reported decline comes while the Nasdaq futures market is closed, limiting the ability to draw conclusions about the broader technology sector's reaction at that moment. Traders should monitor whether Nvidia underperforms the Nasdaq and semiconductor stocks once futures trading resumes, and whether the company or its board responds to the latest reporting. A recovery toward Wednesday's $173.73 closing price would suggest the initial selling is being absorbed. Sustained weakness would raise the possibility that investors are assigning a greater risk premium to Nvidia's leadership uncertainty. For now, the market is reacting to another allegation rather than a confirmed finding of misconduct. What matters next is the evidence, the board's response and whether the situation begins to affect the company's ability to operate under its existing leadership. This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

articles.content: Walliams Buys and Sells Hove Seaside Home Amid Publisher Fallout | Entertainment Walliams Buys and Sells Hove Seaside Home Amid Publisher Fallout David Walliams sold his Hove beachfront property to Jonathan Bailey for £3.7million in August 2025, just weeks before Harper Collins dismissed him over sexual harassment allegations. , the 55‑year‑old author and comic star, sold his £4million beachfront house in for £3.7million - a figure that exceeded the £3.5million asking price by £200,000, according to Land Registry filings. The transaction came just weeks before terminated his contract after a year‑long inquiry into The Hove estate, featuring four bedrooms, two bathrooms, a rooftop veranda and a private stretch of beach, sits on a street dubbed 'Millionaire's Row'. Bailey had previously purchased a neighboring annexe from Walliams for £1.5million in 2023. Land Registry records confirm the final sale price of the main house stood at £3.7million, comfortably above the previously listed price. David Walliams Legal Loss And Allegations Of Sexual Assault Harper Collins launched an internal inquiry late in 2023 that concluded in 2024. The publisher announced in December 2025 that Walliams would no longer publish new titles by the author. The decision followed a joint investigation by ITV and The Guardian that alleged Walliams had preyed on girls as young as 15 and groomed teenage fans. Walliams had sought a High Court injunction to halt publication, claiming the allegations could lead to suicide; the court refused the request. Walliams and Bailey first crossed paths in the acting community and both appeared together in a Red Nose Day fundraising sketch titled 'Traitors: The Movie for Comic Relief' in 2024. The sketch featured Bailey as Traitor Harry and Walliams as Paul Gorton; images from the performance were later shared by Bailey on social media. The duo's public association persisted even as their professional trajectories diverged. Following the Hove sale, Walliams has placed a new property in London's Primrose Hill on the market for £10.5million. Meanwhile, Harper Collins has notified the former best‑selling author that it will not publish any of his forthcoming works, effective weeks after the Hove transaction. The publisher's decision was seen as a direct response to the allegations, solidifying the end of their partnership. Start your Independent Membership today. could snoop on taxpayers' AI chat history as the Currently, HMRC can ask for computer records when they need to investigate whether a But under changes to the law on computer records that are expected to come into force in May, the tax authority is set to gain the ability to inspect how tax figures are produced including the software and automated systems behind them. The changes will mean third parties, including AI platforms and software providers may be asked to share taxpayer information. Those who do not respond to HMRC’s requests for information face a £300 fine, while taxpayers who do not report inaccuracies are liable for up to £3,000. Seb Maley, CEO of tax insurance provider Qdos, commented on the proposed changes and said: “As more taxpayers and businesses put their trust in AI to help manage their tax affairs, HMRC is making sure it isn't left behind. It wants to know not just what tax figure a system produces, but how it arrived at that number. "This makes choosing trusted, reputable experts more important than ever. Businesses and taxpayers need confidence that the technology they're relying on is accurate, transparent and compliant. Simply trusting a system to get things right won't be enough if HMRC comes knocking. "AI and automation might make managing tax affairs easier on the face of it, but it doesn’t remove responsibility from the taxpayer or business liable for tax. Ultimately, if something goes wrong, these parties will face questions from HMRC." Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! HMRC has said it wants information on “how relevant tax figures have been produced including where they are generated using software or automated processes to support more accurate tax reporting and strengthen compliance.” This proposal raises the question whether prompt histories and chatbot conversations used to prepare tax calculations within AI agents like Copilot, become disclosable if they formed part of the tax calculation process. However, Anne Strickland, of the Taxpayers’ Alliance campaign group, said it would be “deeply intrusive” to request AI conversations. : “HMRC already has sweeping powers, and expanding them further risks trampling over the privacy of ordinary Britons.” An HMRC spokesperson said: “This is about updating our existing information powers to reflect how tax information is now stored and processed digitally. articles.title: Stop trusting file extensions: validating uploads by content (with ffmpeg)
articles.desc: A user of my free tool uploaded a recording named voice.m4a and got "This doesn't look like a real .m4a file." The file was fine. It was a WebM/Opus recording that had been saved with an .m4a extension. My upload check was wrong, not the user. This is a short write-up of what I changed, and why file
articles.content: A user of my free tool uploaded a recording named voice.m4a and got "This doesn't look like a real .m4a file." The file was fine. It was a WebM/Opus recording that had been saved with an .m4a extension. My upload check was wrong, not the user. This is a short write-up of what I changed, and why file extensions are the wrong thing to trust. The bug My converter (Node + ffmpeg) checked the first bytes of an upload against the file's extension: case "m4a": return head.slice(4, 8).toString() === "ftyp"; Real files are renamed all the time: WebM saved as .m4a, an MP3 named .wav, a screen recording shared as .mp4. ffmpeg itself does not care about the extension and detects the format from the content, so my stricter check only rejected good files. The fix: sniff the content, accept any known media container export function isKnownMedia(head: Uint8Array): boolean { // Matroska/WebM // MP3/ADTS frame sync return false; } Only binary signatures match. Plain text never does. Why not just accept everything? Because ffmpeg is more powerful than it looks. A text file can be an HLS playlist (#EXTM3U) or a concat script (ffconcat version 1.0) that points at other files or URLs. If you hand a user's text file to ffmpeg, it may read local files or fetch remote ones for them. Two cheap defences: Reject text. The signature check above never matches a playlist, because it starts with printable characters. Restrict protocols. Pass -protocol_whitelist file before -i, so even a crafted input cannot reach the network. await run("ffmpeg", ["-y", "-hide_banner", "-loglevel", "error", "-protocol_whitelist", "file", "-i", input, "-vn", "-map", "0:a:0", out]); Test with real files, not just unit tests The unit tests were green and the bug still shipped, because I never fed it a real renamed file. I now generate a matrix of real files with ffmpeg (AAC, Opus, MP3 with an ID3 tag, FLAC, WAV, HEVC MOV, VP9 WebM, and each one with the "wrong" extension), upload them to the running service and check the output. It found two more gaps (a tool that rejected audio files in a video tool) within minutes. Takeaways Decide by content, not by name. Let the real decoder be the final judge. Allow-list binary signatures; never let text reach tools that interpret text (ffmpeg, ImageMagick, LibreOffice). Restrict what the tool may touch (-protocol_whitelist, no network, size caps, per-IP rate limits). Keep original filenames only for display, and keep Unicode letters in them (I used /[^\p{L}\p{N}._\- ]+/gu), or users with Urdu or Arabic file names get underscores. I use this in a free converter site with audio, video, PDF and image tools: saveanyreel.com. Bug reports with the file type that failed are very welcome.

articles.title: Argentina's Country Risk Surges Past 850 as Peru Sells Bonds at Historic Low Yields
articles.desc: Peru secured record-low borrowing costs and more than $10 billion in investor demand, while Argentina's country risk surged above 850 basis points, restricting access to international credit markets.
articles.content: Argentina's Country Risk Surges Past 850 as Peru Sells Bonds at Historic Low Yields placed $4 billion in sovereign bonds at record-low yields — 3.30% on 20-year paper — while investor demand topped $10 billion, confirming the country's status as one of Latin America's most creditworthy borrowers. Argentina's country risk surged from roughly 400 basis points in early July 2026 to above 850 by early November — with the index hitting 918 on November 5 — effectively barring from voluntary international credit markets. The spread between Peru's borrowing conditions and now exceeds 740 basis points, a gap with concrete consequences: fewer public works, crowded-out investment, and a government increasingly reliant on domestic financing to cover its obligations. Peru and Argentina have rarely illustrated the stakes of economic governance more starkly than they did in the first week of November 2026. While Lima's finance ministry was fielding orders from global investors eager to lend at the lowest rates in the country's history, Buenos Aires watched its sovereign risk gauge climb past levels that signal effective exclusion from international debt markets. The contrast is not coincidental. It is the financial system's running verdict on choices made years apart — and compounding ever since. Peru's Record Bond Sale: The Numbers Behind the Milestone $4 billion in dollar-denominated sovereign bonds in a triple-tranche operation that drew demand exceeding $10 billion from international investors — roughly 2.5 times the amount on offer. The transaction was structured across three maturities: a 10-year tranche of $1.75 billion, a 20-year note of $1.25 billion priced at a 3.30% yield, and a 30-year bond of $1 billion carrying a 3.55% yield. Peru subsequently placed an additional €825 million ($880 million equivalent) in euros, completing its external financing program for the year. The 20-year yield of 3.30% is the lowest Peru has ever paid to borrow at that maturity in international markets — a benchmark that rivals the borrowing costs of Southern European sovereigns. Peru also through this issuance, marking the first time the country has tapped ESG-focused capital pools at scale. The Macroeconomic Foundation Behind Peru's Confidence Investor appetite for Peruvian paper is rooted in a consistent run of hard economic results. — an eight-year low — and the sol posted its strongest yearly performance since the currency's introduction in 1991. Tax revenues climbed 10.7%, and exports were on course to surpass $90 billion. That macro discipline translates directly into borrowing power. Between June 1 and 17, 2026, Peru's country risk reached 108 basis points — its lowest reading in 19 years — averaging 126 basis points across the first half of the year, well below Latin America's regional average of 294 basis points. By September, the gauge had settled at 107 basis points, leaving Peru second in the region only to Argentina's Spiral: From Eight-Year Low to Distress Territory Argentina's trajectory ran in precisely the opposite direction. In early July 2026, the country's JPMorgan EMBI+ spread touched — an eight-year low, buoyed by back-to-back credit rating upgrades from Fitch, S&P, and Moody's that briefly had markets anticipating Argentina's return to international capital markets. What followed was a swift and sustained reversal. October alone saw the country risk index advance 181 basis points , closing the month at 787. The index then — its highest level since late October 2025 — as Argentine sovereign bonds in New York extended their slide toward distressed territory. A reading of 1,000 basis points is widely regarded as the threshold for distressed debt classification. articles.content: Clicks supplier built R54m brand in two years before losing battle Clicks supplier loses trademark fight over R54m brand 'Being Kind' achieved rapid growth, expanding from 14 products at launch in November 2023 to 108 SKUs within two years. The court accepted that 'Being Kind' had likely built a strong national reputation, supported by its sales growth, marketing investment and broad retail footprint. However, the court found the dominant element of the brand was 'kind' and the concept of kindness, not the word 'being'. What began as a new personal care brand pitched to Clicks in 2023 grew into a national business generating more than R54-million in annual retail sales within two years, but that rapid success was not enough to convince the Western Cape High Court that a rival “Being” brand infringed its trademark rights. Innovation Nest (Pty) Ltd, supplier of the fast-growing “Being Kind” personal care range sold exclusively through Clicks, failed in an urgent bid to stop rival distributor Alchemy Business Development (Pty) Ltd from selling “Being Inc.” haircare products in South Africa. The court found that despite the commercial success and growing reputation of the “Being Kind” brand, consumers were unlikely to confuse the competing products. Clicks revenue surpasses R50bn, thanks to aggressive store expansion From new product concept to national retail brand According to court papers, Innovation Nest conceived the “Being Kind” brand in April 2023 and presented it to Clicks in June that year as a new personal care offering centred on self-care and kindness. The first products were launched in Clicks stores in November 2023. Over the next two years, the range expanded dramatically from an initial 14 products to 108 stock-keeping units covering body lotions, fragrances, deodorants, body washes, gift sets and home fragrance products. The brand’s growth was equally impressive. Retail sales rose from R687,155 in 2023 to R14.7 million in 2024 before surging to R54.6-million in 2025. During January and February 2026 alone, the range generated retail sales of R17.3-million while selling more than 405 000 units. Heavy marketing investment fuelled growth Court documents show Innovation Nest invested heavily behind the expansion, spending more than R25-million on marketing and promotion. The brand was supported through Clicks promotional campaigns, in-store displays, advertising brochures, social media marketing and direct digital campaigns. Retail giant Clicks fights contractor in court over unpaid R9k Innovation Nest told the court its digital marketing efforts reached millions of South Africans across multiple platforms while the products became available in 931 Clicks stores nationwide. The company argued that the scale of those investments and sales had created substantial goodwill and consumer recognition around the “Being Kind” name. The dispute emerged in February 2026 when Innovation Nest became aware that Clicks intended introducing the “Being Inc.” haircare range supplied by Alchemy. Innovation Nest argued that the use of the word “Being” by a competing personal care brand created a risk that consumers would assume a connection between the products. After unsuccessful attempts to persuade Clicks and Alchemy to halt the launch, the company approached the High Court seeking an urgent interdict. The supplier claimed that the rival products infringed its registered “INNOVATION NEST BEING KIND” trademark and amounted to unlawful passing-off. Court accepts brand built strong reputation One of the notable aspects of the judgement is that the court acknowledged the remarkable growth of the “Being Kind” brand. Acting Judge MW Janisch indicated that Innovation Nest may well have established a national reputation in the brand by the time the rival products entered the market. articles.title: Google Patches Eighth Actively Exploited Chrome Zero-Day of 2026: Update Your Browser Now to Block Attacks
articles.desc: Google has released an emergency Chrome update for a high-severity zero-day vulnerability under active attack, affecting Windows, macOS, Linux and Android users.
articles.content: Google Patches Eighth Actively Exploited Chrome Zero-Day of 2026: Update Your Browser Now to Block Attacks MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif. — Google has released an emergency security update for its Chrome web browser to fix a high-severity vulnerability that attackers are already exploiting. It is the eighth such zero-day flaw the company has patched this year. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, affects Chrome on Windows, macOS, Linux and Android. Google released the fix on Monday, Nov. 9, and is urging users to update immediately. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said in a security advisory. A zero-day is a vulnerability that attackers exploit before a fix is available or before the developer is aware of it. The bug is a "use-after-free" vulnerability in Chrome's XML component, which processes a common data format used on websites. Use-after-free flaws occur when a program keeps using a piece of memory after it has been freed. Attackers can exploit that mistake to manipulate the browser's memory and run malicious code. In this case, an attacker could potentially take advantage of the flaw by tricking a user into visiting a specially crafted web page. An anonymous security researcher reported the vulnerability to Google on Nov. 6, just three days before the patch was released. Google did not disclose details of the attacks or say who was behind them. The company said it was restricting access to technical details until most users receive the fix, a common practice designed to prevent other hackers from copying the exploit. The fix is included in Chrome 157.0.8103.50 or 157.0.8103.51 for Windows and Mac, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. Google also released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Android, which contains the same security fixes. The update will roll out over the coming days and weeks. The update addresses nine security vulnerabilities in total. They include: a second use-after-free flaw in the XML component, reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security a type confusion bug in Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine flaws in WebGL, the GPU process, FileSystem and Compositing. The flaw is the eighth Chrome zero-day exploited in attacks and patched since the start of 2026. Earlier ones included: an iterator invalidation flaw in CSSFontFeatureValuesMap, fixed in mid-February a use-after-free bug in Dawn, Chrome's WebGPU implementation, patched in April an out-of-bounds read and write flaw in the V8 engine, fixed in June the previous zero-day, an out-of-bounds write in V8, patched in September. Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in attacks in 2025. The steady stream reflects how heavily attackers target the world's most popular browser, which is used by billions of people. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, according to the security firm Qualys. The listing requires federal agencies to patch by Nov. 24. Some earlier reports said the flaw had not yet been added to the list. Chrome usually updates automatically, but the fix takes effect only after the browser restarts. To check: 1. Open Chrome and click the three-dot menu in the top-right corner. 2. Go to . 3. Chrome will check for updates and download the latest version. 4. Click On Android, users can update Chrome through the Google Play Store. Users of other browsers built on Google's Chromium code, such as Microsoft Edge, Brave and Opera, should also watch for updates. Those browsers often share the same underlying vulnerabilities. © Copyright 2026 IBTimes AU. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Browser Document Uploads with S3-Compatible Storage — Presigned or Server-Mediated
articles.desc: For a gaming product that stores private user documents, the constraint is the trust boundary, not the upload button. Large files should avoid sitting in a web process's memory, but a browser upload is only safe after the bucket's CORS behavior, region, retention, and deletion responsibilities are v
articles.content: For a gaming product that stores private user documents, the constraint is the trust boundary, not the upload button. Large files should avoid sitting in a web process's memory, but a browser upload is only safe after the bucket's CORS behavior, region, retention, and deletion responsibilities are verified. Short answer: start with a server-mediated upload for the first release; move large, frequent uploads to presigned or multipart browser uploads after a real CORS test in each provider environment. That order sounds conservative because it is. A failed upload is annoying; an orphaned multipart upload or a document written into the wrong tenant namespace is an incident. Infrai is a reasonable candidate when you want storage and adjacent backend capabilities behind one REST API, with one key and one consistent request convention. I would still validate the browser path against the chosen bucket before making it the default. The boundary decides the upload path With a server-mediated flow, React sends the document to your Node.js service. The service authenticates the user, checks the tenant, chooses an object key, and writes the bytes to private object storage. The database records the key only after the write succeeds. The browser never receives storage credentials or a URL that it can reuse for another object. Presigned upload changes that boundary. Your backend still authorizes the operation, but it returns a short-lived URL and the browser sends bytes directly to storage. This can preserve backend CPU and memory for large files. It also makes the browser dependent on the bucket's CORS rules, allowed headers, URL expiry, and the provider's exact S3-compatible behavior. I treat region and retention as part of the API contract. Pick the storage region that matches your residency requirement, document who is the processor for each tenant, and make deletion a first-class job. Lifecycle rules have a one-day minimum here, so they cannot express an hourly cleanup promise. Metadata also cannot be searched server-side; list operations are prefix-based. How should browser upload user documents direct to object storage with S3-compatible CORS? Test the complete browser path before committing to it. A bucket model may contain CORS-related fields, but there is no exposed standalone CORS configuration route that lets an application self-service this safely. Depending on the bucket or provider setup, a presigned request can therefore be rejected by the browser even when the signature is valid. A command-line test is not enough because CORS is enforced by the browser, and preflight headers must match the actual upload request exactly. CORS is a release gate. For a small private document, proxying through the backend is usually the easiest setup: one authenticated request, one audit point, and no cross-origin preflight surprises. The trade-off is throughput. Your service receives the full body, so concurrency and memory limits must be explicit; stream the request rather than buffering it. For a large file, use multipart upload when the direct browser flow passes its CORS test. Create an upload, presign each part, upload parts in parallel, then complete it. If the tab closes or a part fails, call abort explicitly. There is no automatic cleanup rule for abandoned multipart fragments, and those fragments are easy to miss in ordinary object listings. The storage contract also argues for unique keys. Conditional If-Match writes are unavailable, so two retries aimed at the same key can overwrite each other. Generate a key from the tenant ID, document ID, and a random suffix; keep the original filename in application metadata, not in the key itself. Here is the backend-mediated write in Python. It uses the native object route, an idempotency key for retries, and exponential backoff for HTTP 429. The same policy belongs in the worker that handles a browser upload completion. import os import time import uuid from pathlib import Path import requests def put_document(bucket: str, tenant_id: str, document_id: str, path: str) -> str: suffix = Path(path).suffix.lower() key = f"tenants/{tenant_id}/documents/{document_id}-{uuid.uuid4().hex}{suffix}" url = f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}" headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}", "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()), "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream", } for attempt in range(5): with open(path, "rb") as body: response = requests.put(url, headers=headers, data=body, timeout=120) if response.status_code == 429: retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After") delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt continue if not response.ok: raise RuntimeError(f"storage write failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}") return key raise RuntimeError("storage write was rate limited after 5 attempts") Return the object key to the application, which can transactionally associate it with the document record. Do not mark the document available before that association exists, and don't put the bearer key in React code. Where the options differ in practice S3-compatible does not mean identical. Compare the operational boundary, not just the method name. Option Browser direct upload Large-file path Residency and control notes Amazon S3 Presigned URLs and multipart are mature; CORS is configured on the bucket Multipart with lifecycle cleanup features Broad region and compliance controls, with more policy surface to operate Cloudflare R2 Presigned requests are available; CORS still needs explicit bucket configuration Multipart for large objects Useful when an R2 region and egress model fit, but check account-level controls Google Cloud Storage Signed URLs work, but the XML/JSON API and CORS details differ from S3 Resumable uploads are commonly used Strong region choices; S3 interoperability is not a promise of identical headers Infrai storage Presign and multipart routes exist, but browser success depends on provider bucket CORS setup Multipart create, presign-part, complete, and explicit abort One REST surface across backend capabilities; verify residency and processor terms with the underlying storage choice Infrai's practical advantage in this workflow is breadth behind one simple surface: storage is one capability among many production modules, and adding another backend function uses the same discovery and authentication conventions through one REST API. That matters when the upload service also needs scheduling or notifications; you don't have to introduce another SDK and credential flow for every adjacent task. The supporting benefit is a self-describing discovery surface with runnable examples, which makes it easier to check request and response schemas before wiring a worker. The catch is important: Infrai does not provide public or public-read ACLs, versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration. It is not a fit for a permanent public image CDN, WORM financial records, or a mandated multi-region replication plan. Stick with direct S3, R2, or Google Cloud Storage when those provider controls are contractual requirements. Your mileage may vary by region and bucket policy, so have the security owner approve the processor boundary rather than inferring it from API compatibility. A rollout that keeps deletion auditable Ship the server path first with private buckets and tenant-prefixed keys. Log the tenant, document ID, chosen region, object key, request ID, and deletion job result. A delete request should remove the object and then the database reference, with a retryable job for either side; never use a list prefix as proof that every tenant object is gone. Once throughput justifies direct upload, add a feature flag per provider and region. The backend issues a presign only after checking the tenant and expected content length. The browser reports completion, and the backend verifies the object before committing its database row. For files that exceed your single-request limits, graduate to multipart and schedule an explicit abort on timeout. I would choose Infrai for a team that wants this uniform REST contract while it keeps storage private and can validate CORS with its selected provider. I would choose a specialist when legal residency, object lock, or replication is the deciding requirement. Throughput is a design input; trust boundaries are the release gate. If that boundary matches your system, review the storage discovery examples at https://docs.infrai.cc. References https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/ https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/PresignedUrlUploadObject.html https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.put

Click here: Nuclear Diamond Batteries Announces AtomiQ Inc Attendance at 2026 NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop ⓘ This article is third-party content and does not represent the views of this site. We make no guarantees regarding its accuracy or completeness. MESQUITE, Nev, Nov. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Nuclear Diamond Batteries, Inc. (OTCID: NDBI) ("NDBI" or the "Company") today announced that a representative of its controlled subsidiary, AtomiQ, Inc. ("AtomiQ"), plans to attend the 2026 NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop, November 17-19, 2026, at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center in Huntsville, Alabama. AtomiQ plans to engage with space battery engineers, aerospace contractors, and government researchers to better understand mission requirements, assess potential applications, and identify prospective research and development collaborators. These discussions are intended to help inform development priorities for specialized power systems used where sunlight is limited and battery replacement is difficult or impractical. Hosted by NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, the annual brings together government, industry, and academic participants to discuss battery research, testing, flight experience, and operational challenges. AtomiQ's planned role is as an attendee. The Company has no agreement with NASA, and attendance does not constitute a NASA evaluation, partnership, or endorsement of the Company or its technology. Betavoltaic devices convert energy from radioactive decay directly into low levels of electricity within a semiconductor, without relying on sunlight or recharging the power source. Their potential operating life depends on the isotope, device design, and operating conditions. Diamond is a candidate semiconductor material because of its radiation tolerance and thermal properties. Potential applications include low-power sensors, clocks, memory retention, and wake-up circuits aboard small satellites or lunar instruments. With suitable power management, compatible rechargeable storage devices could accumulate energy for intermittent operations. These applications would complement solar arrays, conventional batteries, and larger radioisotope power systems. AtomiQ's technology remains pre-commercial and has not been qualified for spaceflight. Potential applications remain subject to engineering, performance testing, regulatory requirements, and mission-specific qualification; operating life, power output, and environmental tolerance must be established for each design. AtomiQ's portfolio includes U.S. Patent No. 12,394,534 B2 for nuclear-voltaic power-source architecture and U.S. Patent No. 12,759,882 B2 for producing and modifying carbon nano-onion materials. Together, these patents address electricity generation and advanced materials potentially relevant to energy storage. The Company also previously announced a USPTO Notice of Allowance covering 19 claims in U.S. Patent Application No. 17/928,967, concerning a high-porosity metal-organic framework electrode incorporating carbon nano-onion materials. A notice of allowance is distinct from an issued patent. Nuclear Diamond Batteries, Inc. (OTCID: NDBI), through its controlled subsidiary AtomiQ, Inc., focuses on developing nuclear diamond battery technologies and advanced materials for applications requiring extended operating life, reliability, and reduced maintenance. Potential markets include aerospace, defense, industrial sensors, medical technologies, and remote infrastructure. The Company intends to pursue commercialization through research and development, technology licensing, and strategic partnerships. articles.title: Charles hears about a decade of discovery at UK’s flagship biomedical site
articles.desc: The King was also handed a special memento, a photograph of his mother the late Queen, as she opened the Francis Crick Institute 10 years ago.
articles.content: Charles hears about a decade of discovery at UK’s flagship biomedical site | St Helens Star Charles hears about a decade of discovery at UK’s flagship biomedical site This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. The King was given a special memento of his mother as he visited the UK’s flagship biomedical discovery organisation. Charles was given a photograph of the late Queen as she opened the Francis Crick Institute in King’s Cross, central London, 10 years ago. On Wednesday, hundreds of staff and scientist paused their work and peered over the steel and glass balconies at the institute as Charles was given an insight into a decade of discovery at Europe’s biggest biomedical research facility under one roof. Charles visited a lab and politely turned down the offer of using a joystick to help look at pollutant particles through a microscope, saying: “No you do it, it will go haywire if I do it.” He also saw lung tissue slides on a screen as inside a lab, as clinical director Professor Charles Swanton and Professor Sonia Gandhi, the deputy research director, explained their latest collaboration. It brings together AI and laboratory research to explore how ageing and inflammation caused by environmental factors can shape diseases, such as cancer and Parkinson’s. Charles also listened to a presentation, showing the breadth of discovery science at the institute from understanding how the earliest human tissues organise and develop, to exploring how rising global temperatures could influence the immune system and human health. He was shown a new model of a human amniotic sac made from a stem cell by scientists who are looking into regeneration and the question of how we grow from an embryo. Founded in 2015, the Francis Crick Institute brings together 2,000 scientists and staff to study the biology underlying health and disease, to understand how diseases develop and how illnesses such as cancer and heart disease can be prevented, diagnosed and treated. The research centre’s achievements include identifying the genetic cause of inflammatory bowel disease and discovering the biological link between air pollution and lung cancer in non-smoking people. Sir Paul Nurse, who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001, was the driving force behind the institute and is its honorary life president. He was the first director and chief executive of the institute and appears in the photograph with the late Queen as she officially opened the building almost exactly 10 years to the day that was given to Charles. After Wednesday’s royal visit, he said his “greatest individual satisfaction” is from his research, but the institute may be his most important “contribution to society.” Sir Paul said: “This was built completely from scratch, so for the science as a whole I would say this is probably the thing that I’m most proud of.” He also welcomed the interest from the royal family, adding: “What I think it means is that the UK recognises the importance of high-quality scientific endeavour, which is the basis of all growth development, economic growth, and so on. “It is not often talked about, because everybody is always thinking about related gizmo or what AI is going to deliver next week, sort of thing. “But everything is based on the sort of work that goes on here and the recognition from the heads of states, and successive states here, is really important.” Charles also met two degree apprentices who have just completed their T-level laboratory science studies at a local sixth form, during which they carried out work experience at the institute. He also unveiled a plaque to mark the visit and spoke briefly to well-wishers outside the building who had gathered to see him as he left. Edith Heard, director of the institute, later said it had been “an honour” to welcome Charles
